cases.caseName: Marbury v. Madison
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. Courts may strike down legislative and executive acts that conflict with the Constitution, and a writ of mandamus cannot issue where the statute purporting to grant jurisdiction exceeds Article III.

cases.caseName: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. De jure segregation of children in public schools solely on the basis of race deprives minority children of equal protection of the laws, overruling the separate-but-equal doctrine in public education.

cases.caseName: Gideon v. Wainwright
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and obligatory on the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. An indigent defendant charged with a felony must be appointed counsel at public expense; trials without one are inherently unfair.

cases.caseName: Miranda v. Arizona
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: Custodial interrogation is inherently compelling. Before questioning, police must warn a suspect of the rights to silence and to counsel and honor any assertion of them; statements taken without these safeguards are presumed involuntary and inadmissible in the prosecution's case.

cases.caseName: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: A public official may not recover damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to official conduct unless actual malice is shown by clear and convincing evidence — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of the truth. The First Amendment breathes with a commitment to uninhibited, robust and wide-open debate on public questions.

cases.caseName: Loving v. Virginia
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: Marriage is one of the vital personal rights essential to the orderly pursuit of happiness. Statutes banning interracial marriage rest solely upon invidious racial discrimination and violate equal protection and due process; the freedom to marry cannot be restricted by racial classifications.

cases.caseName: Roe v. Wade
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: A state criminal abortion statute that excepts only life-saving procedures, without regard to pregnancy stage, violates the liberty protected by the Due Process Clause. The decision in Dobbs (2022) later overruled this holding and returned the issue to the States — cite it today as overruled authority or for its continuing persuasive framework.

cases.caseName: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: Where a statute administered by an agency is silent or ambiguous with respect to the specific question, courts must give effect to the agency's interpretation if it reflects a permissible construction — the two-step deference doctrine. Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron: courts must now exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning.

cases.caseName: Nollan v. California Coastal Commission
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: A land-use permit condition that compels an easement must substantially advance a legitimate state interest and be roughly proportionate to the impact of the proposed development; an out-and-out plan of extortion flunks the Takings Clause.

cases.caseName: Dolan v. City of Tigard
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: An exaction must have an essential nexus to a legitimate state interest and be roughly proportional in nature and extent to the impact of the proposed use; the agency bears the burden of showing the required degree of connection.

cases.caseName: Obergefell v. Hodges
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.ratioDecidendi: Same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry in all States, and States must recognize lawful out-of-state marriages; denying that right violates the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses.

cases.caseName: Donoghue v Stevenson
cases.ratioDecidendi: A manufacturer of articles of daily consumption owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer even absent contract. You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour — persons so closely and directly affected by the act.

cases.caseName: Entick v Carrington
cases.ratioDecidendi: Messengers of the Crown may not enter private property to seize papers without positive legal authority. Every invasion of private property, be it ever so minute, is a trespass; the great end of society is that men have a right to their property undisturbed — the seed of modern privacy and search law.

cases.caseName: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
cases.ratioDecidendi: An advertisement offering a reward to anyone who uses a product as directed and still falls ill is a unilateral offer to the world at large; performing the conditions is acceptance. The £1,000 deposited at the bank showed contractual seriousness — no negotiation required, no notice of acceptance needed.

cases.caseName: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd
cases.ratioDecidendi: Goods displayed on a self-service shop shelf are an invitation to treat, not an offer; the contract is concluded at the cash desk when the cashier accepts. Display-plus-price does not bind the shopkeeper, which keeps statutory supervision of restricted sales workable.

cases.caseName: Felthouse v Bindley
cases.ratioDecidendi: Silence or mental reservation cannot amount to acceptance of an offer. An uncle's letter — 'if I hear no more from you, I shall consider the horse mine' — bound nobody: acceptance must be communicated by the offeree, and the nephew's intended silence was no contract.

cases.caseName: Pepper (Inspector of Taxes) v Hart
cases.ratioDecidendi: Parliamentary statements by a Bill's sponsor may be consulted to resolve statutory ambiguity or absurdity, provided the language is unclear and the statements are clear and relied upon by the opposition — the controlled relaxation of the exclusionary rule on legislative history.

cases.caseName: Cundy v Lindsay
cases.ratioDecidendi: A rogue who impersonates a reputable firm induces a contract void for mistake of identity, not merely voidable: title never passes to him, so even an innocent third-party purchaser from the rogue acquires nothing. Fraud aimed at identity leaves the victim's property intact in law.

cases.caseName: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service
cases.ratioDecidendi: Prerogative powers are justiciable and reviewable: exclusion from a labour right in the GCHQ ban failed on procedural fairness — employees had a legitimate expectation of consultation. The three grounds of review are illegality, irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness) and procedural impropriety.

cases.caseName: Google France SARL v Louis Vuitton Malletier SA
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
cases.ratioDecidendi: An internet referencing service does not use a trademark in its own commercial communication when it merely stores a keyword; liability arises only where the advertiser's use itself creates confusion or takes unfair advantage — the platform's own conduct remains neutral.

cases.caseName: Google Spain SL v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) and Mario Costeja González
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
cases.ratioDecidendi: A search engine operator is a controller of personal data it indexes. Where results are inadequate, irrelevant or no longer relevant and not justified by public interest, the individual may demand delisting — the right to be forgotten against the operator, not the original publisher.

cases.caseName: Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Ltd and Maximillian Schrems
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
cases.ratioDecidendi: Mass indiscriminate surveillance in a third country cannot secure an essentially equivalent level of protection. Transfers of personal data rest on standard contractual clauses only where the exporter and importer verify effective safeguards case by case — the Privacy Shield was invalid.

cases.caseName: Maximillian Schrems v Data Protection Commissioner (Schrems I)
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Safe Harbour adequacy decision was invalid: the Directive does not bar a national authority from investigating a third-country transfer even under a Commission decision. Adequacy must be assessed on the ground, in light of the third country's actual practices of access and redress.

cases.caseName: Digital Rights Ireland Ltd v Minister for Communications, Marine and Natural Resources
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Data Retention Directive, requiring wholesale retention of traffic and location data of the entire population, was invalid as a serious interference with privacy and data protection that lacked proportionality — blanket retention must be confined to what is strictly necessary.

cases.caseName: R v Oakes
cases.ratioDecidendi: Limits on Charter rights under section 1 must be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society: a pressing and substantial objective, rational connection, minimal impairment, and proportionality between the salutary effects and the deleterious effects of the measure. The reverse-onus presumption of possession for trafficking flunked.

cases.caseName: R v Van der Peet
cases.ratioDecidendi: Aboriginal rights under section 35(1) protect activities integral to the distinctive culture of the claimant society existing prior to contact. Selling small quantities of fish was not integral in that sense for the Sto:lo claimant — the integral-to-distinctive-culture test governs the existence of the right.

cases.caseName: R v Stinchcombe
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Crown has a legal duty to disclose all relevant information to the defence, whether inculpatory or exculpatory, subject only to a clearly articulated claim of privilege. Nondisclosure is a breach of the fair-trial right under section 7; claims of privilege are reviewed by the trial judge, in camera if necessary.

cases.caseName: R v Jordan
cases.ratioDecidendi: Reasonable trial delay is capped: 18 months in provincial court, 30 in superior court, with a transitional exception only where the delay is clearly the product of a marked and unpredictable change in the system. Beyond the ceiling the delay is presumptively unreasonable and the charge is stayed.

cases.caseName: Mabo v Queensland (No 2)
cases.ratioDecidendi: The common law of Australia recognises native title where the Meriam people's traditional connection to their islands had not been extinguished by the Crown. The fiction of terra nullius is rejected: the land was not empty, its inhabitants' rights did not vanish at settlement.

cases.caseName: Wik Peoples v Queensland
cases.ratioDecidendi: Pastoral leases do not necessarily extinguish native title: rights can coexist, with the leaseholder's rights prevailing in any inconsistency. Native title may survive on land held under statutory lease where the grant did not confer exclusive possession.

cases.caseName: Dietrich v The Queen
cases.ratioDecidendi: A serious criminal trial conducted without counsel for an indigent accused who cannot obtain representation may result in a miscarriage of justice; the trial judge should stay proceedings until counsel is available unless the accused competently insists on proceeding.

cases.caseName: S v Makwanyane and Another
cases.ratioDecidendi: Capital punishment is inconsistent with sections 9 and 10 (life and dignity) and section 11(2) (cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment) of the interim Constitution. Ubuntu — respect for human dignity and community — is a guiding value; the death penalty is struck down for all offences in South Africa.

cases.caseName: Khosa v Minister of Social Development
cases.ratioDecidendi: Excluding permanent residents from social assistance for the aged, disability and child support is unfair discrimination that violates dignity and equality. Permanent residents who have made South Africa their home share the moral claim of citizens to the means of survival; the citizenship line in the benefit statutes falls.

cases.caseName: Glenister v President of the Republic of South Africa
cases.ratioDecidendi: Sections 38, 39 and the constitutional scheme read with international law impose a duty on the State to establish an independent, adequately resourced anti-corruption entity; a unit insufficiently independent of executive control fails the constitutional obligation to combat corruption effectively.

cases.caseName: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
cases.ratioDecidendi: Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is plenary but bounded: it cannot alter the basic structure — the identity and essential features such as judicial review, rule of law, and dignity-based rights. Thirteen judges, decided by the slimmest of margins.

cases.caseName: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right flowing from Article 21. State intrusions must pass a three-part test: legality backed by law, legitimate state aim, and proportionality of the measure to the object — the nine-judge bench overruled the MP Sharma and Kharak Singh privacy holdings.

cases.caseName: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Any procedure depriving a person of personal liberty under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable — not merely enacted. Articles 14, 19 and 21 form a golden triangle; arbitrary executive action fails all three, converting procedural fairness into substantive due process for India.

cases.caseName: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Internet shutdown orders are judicially reviewable and must be published. Indefinite suspension of internet services fails the proportionality test under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); authorities must confine orders in time and territory to what is necessary, with a standing review committee.

cases.caseName: Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation
cases.ratioDecidendi: Eviction of pavement and slum dwellers deprives them of their livelihood, which is part of the right to life under Article 21. Removal requires notice and hearing, and humane relocation consideration — a right to livelihood, not merely property, binds municipal demolition.

cases.caseName: Narmada Bachao Andolan v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Large development projects may proceed where relief and rehabilitation measures are in place pari passu with submergence; oustees' Article 21 rights bind the State to rehabilitate before displacement. The Court retained oversight of the rehabilitation timeline rather than stopping the dam.

cases.caseName: M.C. Mehta v Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
cases.ratioDecidendi: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community; it is strictly and absolutely liable for harm, and the measure of compensation is correlated to its magnitude and capacity to pay. Sovereign immunity offers no escape from this deep-pocket accountability.

cases.caseName: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: The State must take positive measures to identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers. Article 21 obligates decent working conditions, and a letter disclosing bondage is treated as a writ petition — epistolary jurisdiction reaching the powerless without formal pleadings.

cases.caseName: People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Paying construction workers less than the minimum wage is forced labour within Article 23: economic compulsion that leaves no choice vitiates consent. Labour welfare statutes bind contractors and principal employers alike; the State cannot look away from systematic violation on its own projects.

cases.caseName: Carter v Canada (Attorney General)
cases.ratioDecidendi: An absolute prohibition on physician-assisted death deprives competent adults who suffer intolerably from grievous and irremediable conditions of life, liberty and security of the person contrary to section 7, and the deprivation is not justified under section 1 because the blanket ban is overbroad.

cases.caseName: Singh v Minister of Employment and Immigration
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 7 protects every person physically present in Canada: a credible refugee claimant facing return to persecution engages life and security of the person. Fundamental justice required an oral hearing before an independent decision-maker where credibility is determinative — written review alone was not enough.

cases.caseName: Hunter v Southam Inc
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 8 protects people, not places: a reasonable expectation of privacy against unjustified state intrusion. Warrantless searches are presumptively unreasonable; prior authorization by an independent and impartial decision-maker on reasonable and probable grounds is the minimum, and administrative convenience cannot displace it.

cases.caseName: Love v Commonwealth; Thoms v Commonwealth
cases.ratioDecidendi: An Aboriginal Australian who satisfies the Mabo (No 2) tripartite test — biological descent, self-identification, and mutual recognition by the community — is not within 'aliens' under section 51(xix): the ordinary meaning of alien cannot apply to persons whose ties to land and community predate the Constitution. A majority so held.

cases.caseName: Australian Communist Party v The Commonwealth
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Act dissolving the Communist Party and forfeiting its property was invalid: Parliament cannot, in substance, adjudicate guilt and punish an association without judicial process, and recitals of national-security purpose cannot save it. Constitutional limits bind even in emergencies, and implications drawn from the constitutional structure limit legislative power.

cases.caseName: Minister of State for Immigration and Ethnic Affairs v Teoh
cases.ratioDecidendi: Ratification of a treaty by the Executive is a positive statement that it will honour its obligations, capable of founding a legitimate expectation that decision-makers will exercise statutory discretion in conformity with the treaty — absent contrary statutory intent — even though unincorporated treaties do not create binding domestic law.
statutoryProvisions: Convention on the Rights of the Child

cases.caseName: Government of the Republic of South Africa v Grootboom
cases.ratioDecidendi: The state must take reasonable legislative and other measures within available resources to realise the right of access to adequate housing. A programme that leaves the desperate — those with no roof over their heads — without any relief is not reasonable: reasonableness is context-sensitive and must include short-term measures for people in crisis.

cases.caseName: Minister of Health v Treatment Action Campaign (No 2)
cases.ratioDecidendi: A rigid, inflexible policy restricting the provision of nevirapine to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission unreasonably limited section 27: the state must take reasonable measures within available resources and cannot put policy rigidities above the interests of those in need. The state was ordered to remove the research-only restrictions and plan an expansion of the programme.

cases.caseName: Kaunda v President of the Republic of South Africa
cases.ratioDecidendi: There is no general enforceable right to demand specific diplomatic protection, but citizens may request it and the executive's response is reviewable for rationality, bad faith or improper purpose. Foreign affairs are a domain of deference where courts police the legality of the process, not the wisdom of the policy.

cases.caseName: Ram Jawaya Kapur v State of Punjab
cases.ratioDecidendi: The executive power of a State is co-extensive with its legislative power, but the executive cannot make law or take on what is properly legislative business without authority: it may act within fields untouched by legislation, yet where the Constitution or a statute requires a particular procedure, the executive must follow it.

cases.caseName: Vishaka v State of Rajasthan
cases.ratioDecidendi: Sexual harassment at the workplace violates Articles 14, 19 and 21. Pending legislation, the Supreme Court laid down binding Guidelines — drawing on CEDAW as a convention consonant with fundamental rights — defining harassment, requiring complaint committees and redressal mechanisms, and holding employers and institutions responsible for enforcement.

cases.caseName: Minerva Mills Ltd v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which immunized constitutional amendments from review and made fundamental rights subordinate to amendment power, destroyed the basic structure: limited amending power, judicial review, and the balance between Part III and the directive principles are all essential features. Parliament cannot, by exercising a limited power, acquire the power to erase the Constitution's identity.

cases.caseName: Google LLC v Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL)
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber)
cases.ratioDecidendi: The right to de-referencing under the Data Protection Directive cannot in principle extend to all versions of a search engine worldwide: a supervisory authority may require de-listing on all EU domain versions together with measures effectively preventing EU users from reaching the results on non-EU versions, but the balance between data protection and the free flow of information must be assessed against the relevant national legal order — global delisting is not the default.

cases.caseName: UsedSoft GmbH v Oracle International Corp
cases.court: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber)
cases.ratioDecidendi: A software licence granted for an unlimited period in return for a one-off fee is a sale of a copy, and the distribution right is exhausted on first sale even for downloaded programs. The lawful acquirer of a used licence may resell it and the copyright owner cannot oppose — provided the previous copy is made unusable — and the acquirer may re-download the copy from the right-holder's site if the licence agreement so provides.

cases.caseName: Coco v The Queen
cases.ratioDecidendi: Police who enter premises and install a listening device without valid authority commit a trespass, and the resulting evidence may be excluded on public-interest grounds. The principle of legality: courts will not impute to the legislature an intention to interfere with fundamental rights or to negate a statutory requirement of authorization unless that intention is made unmistakably clear.

cases.caseName: Soobramoney v Minister of Health, KwaZulu-Natal
cases.ratioDecidendi: A hospital's dialysis triage policy, allocating scarce machines to patients most likely to benefit, was not a breach of the right to emergency medical treatment or the state's section 27(1)(a) obligations: chronic renal failure is not an emergency within section 27(3), tragic choices forced by scarce resources fall within the domain of reasonable measures, and courts will not second-guess good-faith resource allocations that respect human dignity.

sections.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
sections.principle: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.

sections.title: Legitimate interests
sections.principle: Processing is lawful where necessary for a legitimate interest, unless overridden by the interests or rights of the data subject.

sections.title: Right to erasure
sections.principle: The data subject may obtain erasure of personal data no longer necessary, unlawfully processed, or where consent is withdrawn.

sections.title: Adequacy decisions
sections.principle: Transfers to third countries require an adequacy decision ensuring an essentially equivalent level of protection.

sections.title: Freedom of speech and press
sections.principle: Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press — enforced against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment.

sections.title: Assembly and petition
sections.principle: The right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances, shall not be abridged.

sections.title: Warrants on probable cause
sections.principle: No warrant shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.

sections.title: Reasonableness
sections.principle: The right against unreasonable searches and seizures shall not be violated — the anchor of the exclusionary rule and privacy doctrine.

statutes.citation: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Part I of the Constitution Act 1982
statutes.name: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

sections.title: Guarantee of rights
sections.principle: Charter rights are guaranteed subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

sections.title: Life, liberty and security
sections.principle: Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

sections.title: Trial within a reasonable time
sections.principle: Any person charged with an offence has the right to be tried within a reasonable time.

sections.title: Interpretation compatible with Convention rights
sections.principle: So far as possible, primary and subordinate legislation must be read and given effect in a way compatible with Convention rights.

sections.title: Acts of public authorities
sections.principle: It is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way incompatible with a Convention right, unless primary legislation leaves no choice.

sections.title: Private and family life
sections.principle: Everyone has the right to respect for private and family life, home and correspondence, with interference only as necessary and proportionate.

sections.title: Recognition of native title
sections.principle: Native title is recognised and protected as a common law right that continues where connection and non-extinguishment are established.

sections.title: Definition of native title
sections.principle: Native title means the communal, group or individual rights and interests of Aboriginal peoples or Torres Strait Islanders in relation to land or waters under traditional laws and customs.

sections.title: Claimant application
sections.principle: A claimant application must describe the rights claimed and the factual basis of the asserted traditional connection.

statutes.citation: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996
statutes.name: South African Constitution 1996

sections.title: Equality
sections.principle: Everyone is equal before the law; unfair discrimination on any ground is prohibited, with reasonable affirmative measures permitted.

sections.title: Human dignity
sections.principle: Everyone has inherent dignity and the right to have their dignity respected and protected.

sections.title: Health care, food, water and social security
sections.principle: Everyone has the right of access to social security including appropriate social assistance when unable to support themselves.

sections.title: Equality before law
sections.principle: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws.

sections.title: Life and personal liberty
sections.principle: No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law — read as requiring fair, just and reasonable procedure.

sections.title: Remedies for enforcement
sections.principle: The right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights is itself a fundamental right, with writ powers of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari.

statutes.citation: Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006
statutes.name: Forest Rights Act 2006 (India)

sections.title: Gram sabha as authority
sections.principle: The gram sabha is the authority to initiate the process of determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights.

sections.title: Consent before diversion
sections.principle: Diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes requires recognition of rights and informed consent of the gram sabha, with resettlement safeguards.

sections.title: Duties of holders
sections.principle: Forest right holders are bound to protect forests, wildlife and biodiversity alongside the exercise of their rights.

sections.title: Unconscionable contract
sections.principle: A court may refuse to enforce a contract or clause it finds unconscionable, or enforce the remainder limited to avoid an unconscionable result.

sections.title: Implied warranty of merchantability
sections.principle: Unless excluded, a warranty that goods are merchantable is implied in every contract for sale by a merchant with respect to such goods.

sections.title: Buyer's rights on improper delivery
sections.principle: If goods fail in any respect to conform to the contract, the buyer may reject the whole or accept any commercial unit or units.
